topics.title: Collocations: words that go together
topics.summary: Some word pairs are simply what native speakers say. The alternative may be perfectly logical and still sound wrong, which is why collocation is worth more marks than rare vocabulary.
points: make: a decision, a mistake, a phone call, progress, an effort.
do: homework, the washing-up, business, research, someone a favour.
take: a photo, a break, a risk, part, place.
Record the whole phrase in your notebook, never the single word.

questions.prompt: It's time to ___ a decision.
questions.explanation: English says "make a decision". "Take a decision" exists in formal British English but "make" is far safer and more common.

questions.prompt: She's doing ___ into renewable energy.
questions.explanation: The verb is "do research", and "research" is uncountable, so no article and no plural. Two rules in one short phrase.

questions.prompt: Could you ___ me a favour?
questions.explanation: "Do someone a favour" is fixed. Many learners reach for "make" here because it works in their own language.

questions.prompt: We need to ___ a risk if we want to grow.
questions.explanation: "Take a risk", like "take a chance" and "take responsibility". These belong to the "take" family.

questions.prompt: The project has ___ significant progress.
questions.explanation: "Make progress" is the standard collocation, and it upgrades a sentence considerably compared with "got better".

questions.prompt: Prices have risen ___.
questions.explanation: "Rise sharply" is the natural pairing for a steep increase, and it is exactly the language IELTS Task 1 rewards.

questions.prompt: The film ___ a lasting impression on me.
questions.explanation: "Make an impression" is fixed. "Leave an impression" also works; "give" and "do" do not.

questions.prompt: The conference will ___ place in June.
questions.explanation: "Take place" means happen. "Hold" needs an agent — someone holds a conference — so it cannot follow "will" here without changing the sentence.

topics.title: Everyday phrasal verbs
topics.summary: A phrasal verb is a verb plus a small word that changes its meaning completely. They dominate spoken English, which makes them essential for listening and speaking.
points: The small word changes everything: put off, put up with, put on, put across.
In speaking they sound natural; in formal writing prefer the single-word equivalent.
Many are separable: turn the light on, turn it on — but never "turn on it".
Learn them in a sentence, since the meaning rarely comes from the parts.

questions.prompt: They had to ___ the match because of the snow.
questions.explanation: "Call off" means cancel. "Call up" means telephone or summon, and "call for" means require.

questions.prompt: I can't ___ his constant complaining.
questions.explanation: "Put up with" means tolerate. It takes all three words — dropping "with" changes the meaning entirely.

questions.prompt: The meeting was ___ until next week.
questions.explanation: "Put off" means postpone. Note that "call off" would mean cancelled altogether, not moved.

questions.prompt: She ___ her father — same eyes, same laugh.
questions.explanation: "Take after" means resemble a relative. "Take up" would mean start a hobby, and "take over" means assume control.

questions.prompt: We're ___ milk — can you buy some?
questions.explanation: "Run out of" means the supply is finished. "Run into" means meet by chance.

questions.prompt: Can you ___ what this word means?
questions.explanation: "Look up" means find in a reference. "Look into" means investigate, and "look after" means care for.

questions.prompt: The plane ___ two hours late.
questions.explanation: "Take off" is the aircraft leaving the ground. It also means become suddenly successful.

questions.prompt: In a formal essay, which is the better choice for "find out"?
questions.explanation: Phrasal verbs sound informal in academic writing. "Determine" is the single-word equivalent, and swapping them lifts your register.

topics.title: Word families and word formation
topics.summary: One root gives you four or five words. Knowing the family means you can always produce the form the sentence needs, which is worth more than knowing four unrelated words.
points: Noun endings: -tion, -ment, -ness, -ity, -ance.
Adjective endings: -ful, -less, -ive, -able, -ous, -al.
Adverbs usually add -ly to the adjective.
Negative prefixes: un-, in-, im-, ir-, il-, dis-. The choice depends on the first letter.

questions.prompt: The trial was a complete ___. (succeed)
questions.explanation: After "a complete" the sentence needs a noun, and the noun from "succeed" is "success". "Succession" means a sequence — a different word.

questions.prompt: He behaved ___. (responsible)
questions.explanation: The word describes how he behaved, so it modifies a verb and must be an adverb. Adjectives ending -ble take -bly, not -blely.

questions.prompt: The instructions were ___. (use)
questions.explanation: After "were" the sentence needs an adjective. "Useless" means of no use; the opposite would be "useful".

questions.prompt: Which is the correct negative of "legal"?
questions.explanation: Before an l the prefix in- becomes il-. Similarly im- before m or p (impossible), and ir- before r (irregular).

questions.prompt: Her ___ to the project was enormous. (contribute)
questions.explanation: "Her ___ was enormous" needs a noun for the thing contributed. "Contributor" would be the person, not the contribution.

questions.prompt: The results were ___ inconclusive. (large)
questions.explanation: The word modifies an adjective, so it must be an adverb. "Largely" here means mostly, which is a slightly different sense from "big".

questions.prompt: It is a matter of some ___. (urgent)
questions.explanation: After "some" the sentence needs an uncountable noun. Adjectives ending -ent usually form nouns in -ency: urgent, urgency; frequent, frequency.

questions.prompt: The evidence is ___ with the theory. (consist)
questions.explanation: After "is" the sentence needs an adjective, and "consistent with" is the fixed academic phrase for evidence that agrees with a claim.

topics.title: Academic verbs for writing
topics.summary: The difference between band 6 and band 7 writing is often just verb choice. Precise academic verbs say in one word what a vague verb needs a clause to say.
points: Instead of "show": demonstrate, indicate, reveal, suggest — each is a different strength of claim.
Instead of "say": argue, claim, contend, acknowledge, concede.
Instead of "prove": support, corroborate, substantiate. Very little is actually proved.
Match the verb to how sure you are — overclaiming costs marks.

questions.prompt: The data ___ a link, though it does not prove one.
questions.explanation: "Suggests" is the weakest and most honest of these, which is exactly right when the evidence stops short of proof.

questions.prompt: The second study ___ the earlier findings.
questions.explanation: "Corroborate" means to support with further evidence. "Collaborate" means work together — a common and costly confusion.

questions.prompt: Critics ___ that the policy was never properly funded.
questions.explanation: "Contend" introduces an argued position. "Tell" and "talk" need a person as object and are too informal here.

questions.prompt: The author ___ the limitations of the sample.
questions.explanation: "Acknowledge" means openly admit something that weakens your own case — a hallmark of careful academic writing.

questions.prompt: These figures ___ a steady decline.
questions.explanation: "Indicate" is the standard verb for what data shows. "Inform" and "advise" need a person as their object.

questions.prompt: The results ___ from those of previous studies.
questions.explanation: The sentence needs a verb, and "differ from" is the academic phrasing. Many learners write "are different from", which is correct but weaker.

questions.prompt: The paper ___ three possible explanations.
questions.explanation: "Put forward" means propose. In the most formal register you would write "proposes" or "advances" instead.

questions.prompt: Which verb makes the strongest claim?
questions.explanation: "Establishes" asserts that the matter is settled. Use it only when the evidence genuinely supports that much.

topics.title: Describing change and data
topics.summary: IELTS Task 1 is almost entirely this vocabulary. A candidate who can vary the verb, the adverb and the noun form of a trend will not repeat themselves for 150 words.
points: Up: rise, increase, climb, soar, surge. Down: fall, decline, drop, plummet, dip.
Size: slightly, gradually, steadily, sharply, dramatically.
Verb or noun: "rose sharply" = "a sharp rise". Alternating the two is what stops repetition.
No change: remain stable, level off, plateau, stay constant.

questions.prompt: Sales ___ dramatically after the advertisement.
questions.explanation: "Rise" is intransitive: things rise by themselves. "Raise" needs an object — you raise prices. The past of rise is "rose".

questions.prompt: There was a ___ increase in unemployment.
questions.explanation: Before a noun you need an adjective, so "a sharp increase". The verb version would be "increased sharply".

questions.prompt: Figures ___ at around 40% for the rest of the decade.
questions.explanation: "Remain" is a linking verb, so it takes an adjective, not an adverb — like "remain calm" or "stay quiet".

questions.prompt: Which word describes the steepest fall?
questions.explanation: "Plummet" means to fall very fast and very far. "Dip" is a small temporary fall, and "ease" is gentler still.

questions.prompt: The graph shows a steady ___ in car ownership.
questions.explanation: After "a steady" you need a noun, and the noun from "grow" is "growth".

questions.prompt: Numbers rose ___ 2010 ___ 2015.
questions.explanation: "Rise from X to Y" is the pattern for values. "Between 2010 and 2015" would describe the period, not the movement.

questions.prompt: After 2018 the figure ___ off at 25%.
questions.explanation: "Level off" means to stop changing and hold steady. "Plateau" is the one-word alternative.

questions.prompt: The rate fell ___ five per cent.
questions.explanation: "Fell by" gives the size of the change; "fell to" would give the final value. Confusing the two reverses your meaning.

topics.title: Words that are easy to confuse
topics.summary: These pairs look or sound alike but mean different things. They are marked strictly, because using the wrong one usually makes the sentence say something you did not intend.
points: affect (verb) / effect (noun) — the rain affected the crop; the effect was severe.
practice (noun) / practise (verb) in British English.
economic (to do with the economy) / economical (cheap to run).
principal (main, or head of a school) / principle (a rule or belief).

questions.prompt: The weather badly ___ the harvest.
questions.explanation: "Affect" is the verb and "effect" is the noun. A quick test: if you can put "the" in front, you want "effect".

questions.prompt: This car is very ___ — it barely uses any fuel.
questions.explanation: "Economical" means cheap to run. "Economic" relates to the economy as a whole — economic growth, economic policy.

questions.prompt: The ___ reason for the delay was funding.
questions.explanation: "Principal" means main. "Principle" is a rule or belief, as in "a matter of principle".

questions.prompt: You need to ___ every day to improve.
questions.explanation: In British English the verb is "practise" with an s and the noun is "practice" with a c. American English uses "practice" for both.

questions.prompt: The number of applicants has ___ risen.
questions.explanation: An adverb is needed to modify "risen". Note "considerate" means kind and thoughtful — an entirely different word from "considerable".

questions.prompt: She gave a ___ account of what happened.
questions.explanation: "Historical" means relating to the past. "Historic" means important enough to be remembered — a historic victory.

questions.prompt: The two versions are almost ___.
questions.explanation: After "are" the sentence needs an adjective. "Identically" would modify a verb: they are identically packaged.

questions.prompt: Fewer or less? "There were ___ people than last year."
questions.explanation: "Fewer" goes with countable nouns like people; "less" goes with uncountables like money or time.

topics.title: Linking ideas precisely
topics.summary: Linking words are marked on whether they express the right relationship, not on how many you use. A well-chosen "whereas" beats three scattered "moreover"s.
points: Contrast: however, whereas, nevertheless, on the other hand.
Cause: because, since, as, owing to, due to.
Result: therefore, consequently, as a result, thus.
"Despite" and "in spite of" take a noun or -ing; "although" takes a full clause.

questions.prompt: ___ the rain, the match went ahead.
questions.explanation: "Despite" is followed by a noun. "Although" would need a clause: although it was raining.

questions.prompt: Sales rose in the north, ___ they fell in the south.
questions.explanation: "Whereas" joins two contrasting halves inside one sentence. "However" would need a full stop or semicolon before it.

questions.prompt: The road was closed. ___, we had to turn back.
questions.explanation: This is a result, so "therefore". Note the full stop before it — "therefore" cannot join two clauses on its own.

questions.prompt: ___ of the cost, the scheme was abandoned.
questions.explanation: "Because" needs a clause; "owing to" and "due to" take a noun. The trick is to look at what follows, not what you mean.

questions.prompt: Which is correct?
options: Despite it was late, we continued.
Despite of the delay, we continued.
Despite that it was late, we continued.
questions.explanation: "Despite" takes a noun directly — no "of", no clause. "In spite of" is the version that keeps the "of".

questions.prompt: The results were poor. ___, the funding was withdrawn.
questions.explanation: The withdrawal follows from the poor results, so a result linker is needed. "Nevertheless" would signal the opposite relationship.

questions.prompt: He had little experience. ___, he got the job.
questions.explanation: The outcome is surprising given the reason, which calls for a contrast linker. The other three all signal a result.

questions.prompt: ___ working late, she never seemed tired.
questions.explanation: "Working" is an -ing form, and "despite" accepts one. "Although" would need a subject and verb: although she worked late.

topics.title: Talking about people and character
topics.summary: Describing people comes up in almost every speaking test. Precise character adjectives lift a Part 2 answer far above "nice" and "very good".
points: Positive: generous, patient, reliable, easy-going, thoughtful, determined.
Negative: stubborn, arrogant, impatient, unreliable, self-centred.
Careful: "sensible" means having good judgement; "sensitive" means easily hurt.
Give an example after the adjective — that is what turns a word into a band.

questions.prompt: He always arrives when he says he will. He's very ___.
questions.explanation: "Reliable" means you can depend on them. "Sensible" would describe good judgement rather than dependability.

questions.prompt: She refuses to change her mind about anything. She's ___.
questions.explanation: "Stubborn" is the negative version; "determined" is the positive one. The refusal to reconsider is what makes it stubborn.

questions.prompt: He gets upset very easily — he's quite ___.
questions.explanation: "Sensitive" means easily affected emotionally. "Sensible" is a classic false friend that means practical and level-headed.

questions.prompt: Nothing bothers her; she's very ___.
questions.explanation: "Easy-going" means relaxed and tolerant. Note the hyphen — it is a single compound adjective.

questions.prompt: He never stops talking about himself. He's ___.
questions.explanation: "Self-centred" means interested only in oneself. "Self-conscious" means embarrassed about how others see you — nearly the opposite.

questions.prompt: She's willing to wait as long as it takes. She's ___.
questions.explanation: After "is" you need the adjective "patient". "Patience" is the noun: she has a lot of patience.

questions.prompt: He gives a lot of his time to others — he's very ___.
questions.explanation: "Generous" covers giving money, time or praise. "Genuine" means sincere, and "genius" is a noun.

questions.prompt: Which upgrades "He is a nice person" for a speaking test?
options: He is a very nice person.
He's thoughtful — he always remembers what you told him.
He is a nice and good person.
questions.explanation: A precise adjective plus a concrete example is what raises the score. Repeating or intensifying "nice" adds nothing to lexical resource.

topics.title: Hedging and cautious academic language
topics.summary: Hedging softens a claim so it matches the strength of your evidence. Overclaiming what limited evidence shows costs marks just as much as underclaiming what strong evidence shows.
points: Hedging softens a claim so it matches the strength of your evidence.
Common hedges: may, might, tend to, appear to, seems to, is likely to, to some extent.
Overclaiming with "proves" or "always" when evidence is limited costs marks in academic writing.
A hedge can sit on the verb (may increase) or on the whole claim (it is possible that).

questions.prompt: The data ___ suggest a link, but further research is needed.
questions.explanation: "Would" softens the claim to a cautious possibility, matching evidence that is not yet conclusive.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is the most appropriately hedged?
options: This proves that diet causes the illness.
This shows that diet causes the illness.
This may indicate a link between diet and the illness.
This means diet causes the illness.
questions.explanation: "May indicate a link" matches limited evidence. The others all overclaim certainty the evidence does not support.

questions.prompt: Smaller classes ___ to improve results, though the effect varies.
questions.explanation: "Tend to" signals a general pattern rather than an absolute rule, which fits the qualification that follows.

questions.prompt: The policy ___ have contributed to the decline, among other factors.
questions.explanation: "May have" is a cautious past hedge, appropriate when other factors are also acknowledged.

questions.prompt: To ___ extent, the results confirm the theory.
questions.explanation: "To some extent" is a fixed hedging phrase meaning partly, not completely.

questions.prompt: The findings ___ to support the original hypothesis.
questions.explanation: "Appear to" is cautious phrasing; the other options claim more certainty than research findings usually justify.

questions.prompt: It is ___ that costs will rise further next year.
questions.explanation: "Likely" hedges a prediction appropriately. The other words claim near-total certainty about the future.

questions.prompt: Which is the most cautious way to introduce a claim?
questions.explanation: "It could be argued that" openly frames the claim as one interpretation, leaving room for other views — the hallmark of hedged academic writing.

topics.title: Describing quantity and proportion
topics.summary: Task 1 writing lives on this vocabulary. Precise proportion words let you report figures without repeating the same tired phrases.
points: Use "the majority of" and "a minority of" for most/fewest of a group.
"Approximately", "roughly" and "just over/under" describe numbers close to, but not exactly, a figure.
A fraction like "a quarter of" or "two-thirds of" takes the verb form that matches the noun after "of".
Avoid vague words like "a lot" or "loads" in formal writing — prefer "a substantial number" or "a considerable proportion".

questions.prompt: ___ of respondents said they were satisfied with the service.
questions.explanation: "The majority of" is the standard phrase for describing more than half of a group.

questions.prompt: Just ___ half of the students passed the test.
questions.explanation: "Just under" means slightly less than the figure given — a precise way to describe an approximate proportion.

questions.prompt: ___ of the budget was spent on marketing.
questions.explanation: "A quarter of" is the standard way to express one part in four.

questions.prompt: Roughly ___ of the population lives in urban areas.
questions.explanation: Fractions above one are hyphenated and the denominator stays singular: "two-thirds".

questions.prompt: Which is the most formal way to describe a large amount in an essay?
questions.explanation: "A substantial amount of" is precise and formal, unlike the casual alternatives, which suit spoken English better.

questions.prompt: Only a small ___ of employees opposed the change.
questions.explanation: "A small minority of" describes a small proportion of a group opposed to something.

questions.prompt: The figure rose to ___ 3 million by the end of the year.
questions.explanation: "Approximately" is the standard formal word for a number that is close to, but not exactly, the one given.

questions.prompt: ___ half of those surveyed had never travelled abroad.
questions.explanation: "Nearly" is the correct adverb meaning "almost". "Almostly" is not a word, and "near" is not used this way before a fraction.

topics.title: Adjective + preposition collocations
topics.summary: Adjectives, like verbs, pair with a fixed preposition rather than a logical one. A small shift in preposition can also shift the meaning slightly.
points: Many adjectives pair with one fixed preposition: interested in, afraid of, good at, similar to.
The preposition can change with a small shift in meaning: married to, angry with a person, angry about a situation.
After the preposition, use a noun or -ing form, never a bare infinitive.
Learn these as fixed pairs — they rarely follow a predictable pattern.

questions.prompt: She's always been interested ___ languages.
questions.explanation: "Interested in" is the fixed pairing for a subject that appeals to someone.

questions.prompt: I'm not very good ___ remembering names.
questions.explanation: "Good at" is the standard pairing for skills and abilities.

questions.prompt: He's afraid ___ spiders.
questions.explanation: "Afraid of" is the fixed pairing for fears.

questions.prompt: This design is very similar ___ the last one.
questions.explanation: "Similar to" is the fixed pairing for comparisons.

questions.prompt: She was angry ___ her colleague for missing the deadline.
questions.explanation: "Angry with" is used for a person; "angry about" is used for a situation or event.

questions.prompt: The results are consistent ___ earlier studies.
questions.explanation: "Consistent with" is the fixed academic pairing meaning "in agreement with".

questions.prompt: He is capable ___ finishing the task alone.
questions.explanation: "Capable of" is the fixed pairing in English, and the verb after it takes the -ing form, not the infinitive.

questions.prompt: I'm not satisfied ___ this explanation.
questions.explanation: "Satisfied with" is the fixed pairing for an explanation, result or outcome.

topics.title: Everyday and academic register pairs
topics.summary: Casual and formal English often express the same idea with different words. Matching register to the task — an email versus an essay — is part of what examiners are marking.
points: Many ideas have a casual word and a more formal equivalent: kids/children, get/receive, a lot of/numerous.
Contractions (don't, it's, can't) belong in speech, not in formal writing.
Phrasal verbs like "find out" often have a formal one-word equivalent: "determine".
Register is about matching the word to the task, not about one word being "better" than another.

questions.prompt: Which is the more formal way to say "kids"?
questions.explanation: "Children" is the neutral, formal word. The others are all casual or overly familiar.

questions.prompt: In a formal essay, "a lot of people" is better replaced with:
questions.explanation: "Numerous" is the formal equivalent of "a lot of" and fits academic writing, unlike the casual alternatives.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is written in the more formal register?
options: It cannot be said with certainty.
We just don't know for sure.
questions.explanation: The formal version avoids the contraction and uses precise, impersonal phrasing.

questions.prompt: The formal equivalent of "find out" is:
questions.explanation: "Determine" is the single-word academic equivalent; the others are informal phrasal verbs.

questions.prompt: Which is the more formal way to say "get"?
questions.explanation: "Receive" is neutral and formal; the other options are casual synonyms for "get".

questions.prompt: In academic writing, "big" is often better replaced with:
questions.explanation: "Substantial" is precise and formal. The others are informal intensifiers more suited to speech.

questions.prompt: Which is the more formal version of "start"?
questions.explanation: "Commence" is the formal register equivalent of "start" used in reports and academic writing.

questions.prompt: The casual phrase "sort out a problem" is best replaced in writing with:
questions.explanation: "Resolve" is the precise, formal verb for solving a problem in academic or report writing.

topics.title: Education vocabulary
topics.summary: Education comes up constantly in speaking and writing tasks. Precise words for stages, qualifications and money make an answer sound informed rather than vague.
points: Learning happens across stages: primary, secondary, higher education.
"Curriculum" is what is taught; "syllabus" is the more detailed content list for one course.
"Tuition fees" are what you pay; a "scholarship" or "grant" covers some or all of it.
Distinguish "teach" (give lessons) from "study" (learn a subject) — a common confusion.

questions.prompt: After finishing secondary school, many students go on to ___ education.
questions.explanation: "Higher education" is the standard term for university-level study.

questions.prompt: She won a ___ that covers all her tuition fees.
questions.explanation: A scholarship is money awarded for merit that does not need to be repaid, unlike a loan.

questions.prompt: The course ___ covers grammar, writing and speaking skills.
questions.explanation: A "syllabus" lists the specific content of one course, while a "curriculum" refers to the whole programme of study.

questions.prompt: He's ___ medicine at university.
questions.explanation: "Studying" means learning a subject as a student. "Teaching" would mean he gives the lessons.

questions.prompt: Universities often charge high ___ for international students.
questions.explanation: "Tuition fees" is the standard term for the cost of taking a course.

questions.prompt: She got a ___ in economics from a top university.
questions.explanation: "Degree" is the standard word for the university qualification awarded after several years of study.

questions.prompt: Which word means someone doing research for a higher degree?
questions.explanation: A "postgraduate" studies after already completing a first degree, often towards a master's or doctorate.

questions.prompt: He failed the module and had to ___ it the following year.
questions.explanation: "Resit" is the standard term for taking an exam or module again after failing.

topics.title: Environment and sustainability vocabulary
topics.summary: Environmental topics appear regularly in Writing Task 2 and speaking. Precise verbs for harm and protection carry more weight than vague words like "bad for the planet".
points: "Sustainable" describes something that can continue without running out or causing lasting harm.
"Emissions" are gases released, especially from vehicles and industry; "carbon footprint" is the total amount one person or activity produces.
"Renewable" energy comes from sources that do not run out, like solar or wind; "fossil fuels" do.
Verbs of harm and protection: deplete, degrade, conserve, preserve, offset.

questions.prompt: Solar and wind are examples of ___ energy.
questions.explanation: "Renewable" describes energy sources that naturally replenish, unlike fossil fuels, which are finite.

questions.prompt: Factories are being urged to cut their carbon ___.
questions.explanation: "Carbon emissions" refers to the gases released into the atmosphere, especially carbon dioxide.

questions.prompt: Overfishing has severely ___ fish stocks in the region.
questions.explanation: "Deplete" means to reduce a resource until little is left. "Preserve" and "conserve" mean the opposite — to protect it.

questions.prompt: Many companies now try to ___ their emissions by planting trees.
questions.explanation: "Offset" means to balance out one effect, such as emissions, with an equivalent counteracting action.

questions.prompt: The forest has been badly ___ by illegal logging.
questions.explanation: "Degrade" means to reduce the quality of something, here the forest's condition.

questions.prompt: A ___ development approach tries to meet current needs without harming future generations.
questions.explanation: "Sustainable" describes an approach that can continue long-term without depleting resources.

questions.prompt: The government introduced a scheme to ___ endangered species.
questions.explanation: "Conserve" means to protect something from being lost or damaged, which fits protecting a species.

questions.prompt: Coal and oil are known as ___ fuels because they cannot be replaced once used.
questions.explanation: "Fossil fuels" formed over millions of years and are not replaceable on a human timescale, unlike renewable sources.

topics.title: Giving and softening opinions
topics.summary: Speaking tests reward a range of opinion phrases, not just repeated "I think". Softer phrases also let you disagree politely without sounding blunt.
points: Direct opinion phrases: I think, I believe, in my view, as far as I'm concerned.
Softer phrases for disagreement: I see your point, but…; I'm not sure I agree…
"Personally" adds emphasis that the opinion is your own, not a general fact.
Overusing "I think" sounds repetitive — vary the phrase across a speaking answer.

questions.prompt: Which phrase introduces a personal opinion?
questions.explanation: "In my view" clearly signals a personal opinion rather than a stated fact or reported data.

questions.prompt: Which is the most polite way to disagree?
options: I see your point, but I'm not sure I agree.
questions.explanation: This phrase acknowledges the other person's view before disagreeing, which is a polite and natural way to differ.

questions.prompt: ___, I think public transport should be free.
questions.explanation: "Personally" is the adverb used to introduce a strongly individual opinion.

questions.prompt: Which phrase best introduces an opinion in a discussion?
questions.explanation: "As far as I'm concerned" is the correctly formed fixed phrase for introducing a personal viewpoint.

questions.prompt: To agree strongly with someone, you could say:
questions.explanation: "I couldn't agree more" is the fixed idiom for expressing strong agreement.

questions.prompt: Which phrase suggests you have not fully made up your mind?
questions.explanation: "I'm inclined to think" signals a leaning opinion rather than firm certainty, unlike the other phrases.

questions.prompt: Which phrase is too informal for a formal speaking test answer?
questions.explanation: "I reckon" is casual spoken slang. The other phrases suit a more neutral or formal register.

questions.prompt: To politely introduce a different opinion, you can say:
questions.explanation: This phrase disagrees while staying courteous, unlike the blunt or dismissive alternatives.

topics.title: Technology vocabulary
topics.summary: Technology topics reward precise verbs for change and precise nouns for devices, rather than the vague "stuff" and "things" that flatten a Task 2 essay.
points: "Digital divide" describes unequal access to technology between groups.
Verbs for tech change: automate, digitise, streamline, upgrade.
"Innovative" describes something new and original; "obsolete" describes something outdated and no longer used.
Be precise: "device" is general, but "smartphone", "tablet" and "laptop" are more exact when the context allows.

questions.prompt: Many routine tasks have now been ___ by software.
questions.explanation: "Automate" means to make a process run by machine rather than by a person — the standard word for this kind of change.

questions.prompt: The company plans to ___ its filing system by scanning all paper records.
questions.explanation: "Digitise" means to convert something into digital form, which fits scanning paper records.

questions.prompt: The ___ between those with internet access and those without remains a serious issue.
questions.explanation: "Digital divide" is the fixed term for unequal access to technology between different groups.

questions.prompt: This model of phone is now considered ___; nobody makes parts for it anymore.
questions.explanation: "Obsolete" means outdated and no longer in use or supported — the opposite of "cutting-edge" or "innovative".

questions.prompt: The new app is designed to ___ the process of booking appointments.
questions.explanation: "Streamline" means to make a process simpler and more efficient.

questions.prompt: She works for a highly ___ start-up known for original ideas.
questions.explanation: "Innovative" describes something new and creatively different, fitting a start-up known for original ideas.

questions.prompt: Which word best replaces "device" when referring specifically to a phone?
questions.explanation: "Smartphone" is the precise term; "device" is the vaguer, more general word.

questions.prompt: The company decided to ___ all its computers to the latest software.
questions.explanation: "Upgrade" means to improve something, such as software or hardware, to a newer version.

topics.title: Cause, effect and correlation language
topics.summary: Task 2 essays need precise verbs for how one thing leads to another. Confusing cause with correlation, or affect with effect, weakens an argument even when the content is strong.
points: "Lead to", "result in" and "give rise to" all introduce a result; the subject of the verb is the cause.
"Stem from", "arise from" and "be attributed to" work the other way: the subject is the result, and the cause follows.
A correlation is not the same as a cause — two things happening together is not proof that one caused the other.
"Affect" is the verb; "effect" is usually the noun, seen after "have an" or "the".

questions.prompt: Rising fuel prices ___ a sharp increase in public transport use.
questions.explanation: "Lead to" introduces the result that follows the cause; the fuel prices are the cause here, so the effect follows the verb.

questions.prompt: The rise in obesity ___ changes in diet and lifestyle.
questions.explanation: "Be attributed to" puts the result first and the cause after; here the obesity (result) is explained by the changes (cause).

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly distinguishes correlation from causation?
options: Ice cream sales and drowning rates rise together, so ice cream causes drowning.
Ice cream sales and drowning rates rise together, but this does not prove one causes the other.
Because ice cream sales rise, drowning rates must rise too.
Ice cream sales prove that drowning rates will increase.
questions.explanation: A correlation shows two things changing together, but it does not on its own prove that one causes the other — a common flaw examiners look for in Task 2 arguments.

questions.prompt: Poor sleep ___ lower concentration levels the next day.
questions.explanation: "Result in" introduces the effect after the cause; poor sleep is the cause, so it takes the verb that points forward to the result.

questions.prompt: The delay ___ a shortage of staff.
questions.explanation: "Was caused by" is passive and puts the result (the delay) first, with the cause introduced afterwards.

questions.prompt: The weather badly ___ the harvest, and the ___ was a poor yield.
questions.explanation: "Affect" is the verb describing the influence; "effect" is the noun describing the result of that influence.

questions.prompt: Which verb best introduces a cause you are not fully certain of?
questions.explanation: "May have contributed to" hedges the claim, useful when a cause is plausible but not proven — exactly the caution academic writing rewards.

questions.prompt: Economic growth and rising life expectancy often ___, though the exact relationship is complex.
questions.explanation: "Correlate" describes two things changing together without claiming that one causes the other.

topics.title: Paraphrasing: everyday and academic synonyms
topics.summary: Reading and Listening test whether you can match an everyday word in the question to its academic equivalent in the passage. Building a mental list of these pairs is the single most useful preparation for both.
points: Passages often use a more formal or precise word for an idea the question states plainly.
Learn synonym pairs both ways: the everyday word and its academic partner.
A paraphrase changes the words but keeps the meaning exactly — it is not a looser, related idea.
Watch for word-form changes too: a verb in the question may appear as a noun in the passage.

questions.prompt: The question says "get better". Which word in a passage most likely paraphrases it?
questions.explanation: "Improve" means the same as "get better" — a direct paraphrase — while the other options mean something different or opposite.

questions.prompt: Which word means the same as "show" in an academic passage?
questions.explanation: "Demonstrate" is the formal equivalent of "show" — the meaning is the same, only the register changes.

questions.prompt: The question asks about a "big change". Which passage phrase is the closest paraphrase?
questions.explanation: "A significant shift" matches the size and type of change described as "big" in the question; the others describe something smaller or different.

questions.prompt: Which word pairs with "start" as an academic paraphrase?
questions.explanation: "Commence" is the formal equivalent of "start". The others describe different stages of an event.

questions.prompt: The question says "most people agree". Which is the closest paraphrase?
questions.explanation: "Broad consensus" means widespread agreement, matching "most people agree" in meaning, not just in topic.

questions.prompt: Which word means the same as "enough" in formal writing?
questions.explanation: "Sufficient" is the formal paraphrase of "enough" — both mean an adequate amount, unlike the other options.

questions.prompt: The question refers to a "drop in numbers". Which passage phrase paraphrases it?
questions.explanation: "A decline in figures" paraphrases "a drop in numbers" — same direction of change, different words.

questions.prompt: Which is a true paraphrase, rather than a related but different idea?
options: "The policy was postponed" paraphrased as "The policy was delayed."
"The policy was postponed" paraphrased as "The policy was cancelled."
"The policy was postponed" paraphrased as "The policy was approved."
"The policy was postponed" paraphrased as "The policy was popular."
questions.explanation: "Delayed" means exactly the same as "postponed". The other options change the meaning rather than just the wording.
